catalog_quote: Lee p. 34: "It should be noted that the pretonic reflexes of voiced stops in CGR are without aspiration and the same is true in Haroi. Haroi does have an occasional allophonic aspiration of voiceless stops in pretonic position, but is unrelated to the source of the stop (Mundhenk and Goschnick 1977:5ff.). It would also be parallel to Utsat, which has voiceless aspirated stops reflecting original voiced stops in the tonic syllable (e.g. Maddieson and Pang 1993)." Lee p. 47: "To my knowledge only ECham and CGR share the shift of PC *s- to tʰ- and that only in the tonic syllable." Thurgood p. 61 (Proto-Chamic, not CGR-specific): "this pre-Chamic Austronesian (An) language adopted the main-syllable stress of the neighbouring MK languages ... the formerly disyllabic morphemes came to have an unstressed initial syllable followed by a stressed main syllable. This iambic PC stress pattern is certainly reflected in the contrasts between the vowel inventories of the pre-syllable and the main syllable."

new_statements.rule_in_words: IMPLICIT ONLY. Lee never states where stress falls; he labels the presyllable of sesquisyllabic words the 'pretonic syllable' and the main (word-final) syllable the 'tonic syllable' (pp. 33, 34, 35, 47, 49), the standard Chamic/Mainland-SEA usage in which the final main syllable carries the stress and the presyllable is unstressed (with neutral vowel duration, p. 35). Read as: stress on the main = final syllable of the word; presyllables unstressed. The explicit family-level statement is Thurgood 1998 in the same volume, p. 61 (Proto-Chamic iambic: unstressed initial syllable + stressed main syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: None; no stress discussion at all. Lee notes (p. 33) that CGR appears to be developing a Cham-type register system from initial voiced stops, and that the pretonic syllable has neutral vowel duration (p. 35).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, sesquisyllabic (presyllable + main syllable) words in elicited citation forms; data from about two hours of elicitation in 1974, which Lee calls 'very sketchy and some of it not completely reliable phonetically' (p. 31). 'Tonic' here is the SEA-linguistics term for the stressed main syllable, not a claim of lexical tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Lee 1998 describes the speech of two hamlets, Ap Cat Gia and Ap Binh Nghia-Cham (Xa Cat Rai, north of Phan Rang, Ninh Thuan), recorded in 1974; speakers call themselves Radlai. Lee explicitly does not treat it as a Southern Roglai dialect (sout3010) and contrasts it throughout with Northern Roglai (nort2994); it shares the Roglai final-nasal denasalisation but is otherwise Cham-like (register, *s- > th-). Glottolog cacg1235 = ISO roc = the 'Cac Gia' dialect of Cobbey 1977's four-way Raglai split. Data quality caveat from the author himself: ~2 hours of elicitation, 'very sketchy'.

new_statements.quote: Throughout the history of Chamic, there is a clearly-marked, continual movement from disyllabic to iambic and from iambic to monosyllabic, but the initial impetus for these changes was the PC shift to a preference for final stress under MK influence. Once the canonical preference was set for stress on the final syllable, the preconditions had been set up for the restructuring of the Chamic lexicon. [p. 61] ... In this interpretation, contact with MK led to a shift of preference from penultimate to ultimate stress, rather than introducing an entirely new stress pattern. [pp. 61-62] ... Chamic developed word-final stress, leading to the proliferation of contrasts in the stressed final syllable and eventually to the reduction of contrasts in the unstressed syllable. [p. 105-106]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level only: Proto-Chamic, under Mon-Khmer contact, shifted its preference from penultimate to ultimate (main-syllable) stress; all Chamic languages, Roglai included, have final stress on the main syllable of the iambic (sesquisyllabic) word, the pretonic presyllable being unstressed and reduced. The book never states a stress rule for Cat Gia Roglai specifically; it names Cat Gia Roglai (Lee 1998) / Cac Gia Roglai (Cobbey 1977) only in the subgrouping discussion, and Google Books finds no page pairing 'Cat Gia' with 'stress', 'tonic' or 'final syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the statement is diachronic and family-wide (penultimate stress retained only in Malay-type systems outside Chamic)
new_statements.identity_note: Thurgood 1999 treats Cat Gia Roglai (Lee 1998) / Cac Gia Roglai (Cobbey 1977) as a distinct Roglai variety in its subgrouping chapter (index pp. 217, 224-227) but makes its stress statements for Proto-Chamic and Chamic generally, with Roglai named only as a language that kept the presyllable three-way vowel distinction. The existing statement's Lee 1998 is the Cat Gia (Cac Gia) variety of Khanh Hoa, which Lee keeps apart from Southern Roglai.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level, historical statement: Proto-Chamic shifted (under Mon-Khmer contact) from a Malay-like system with mostly penultimate stress to stress on the final (main) syllable of the word; the Chamic languages have word-final stress, with contrasts proliferating in the stressed final syllable and reduced in the unstressed presyllable. Nothing is said about Cat Gia Roglai stress specifically in any visible snippet (feed queries pairing 'Cat Gia' with stress/stressed/unstressed/presyllable/tonic/'final syllable' return 0 entries).
new_statements.exceptions: Only historical: the pre-shift (Malayic-type) system had 'penultimate stress in the vast majority of disyllabic words but ultimate stress in a small group of words' (p. 61); '. Roglai, the presyllable still shows a three-way [vowel] distinction in certain environments' (Northern Roglai, reduction of the unstressed syllable incomplete). No synchronic exceptions for Cat Gia Roglai.
new_statements.identity_note: Thurgood 1999 treats Cat Gia Roglai (Lee 1998) = Cac Gia Roglai (Cobbey 1977) only in its subgrouping discussion (pp. 217-227), as a Roglai dialect 'considerably different from other Roglai dialects'; its stress statements are about Proto-Chamic / Chamic as a whole (data languages: Acehnese, Rade, Jarai, Chru, Northern Roglai, Tsat, Haroi, Western and Phan Rang Cham), not about Cat Gia Roglai as such.
